method_note: All facts gathered via web search on 2026-11-14. Direct page fetches were blocked by the session network (iowapublicradio.org, kcci.com, dmww.com refused), so no page was opened in full. Following the repo's evidence_priors convention, any number not read on the opened original is 'secondary'. source_kind says whether the publisher is the primary body (primary_publisher), news, a third party, or our own arithmetic (derived). Quotes are search-extracted; re-check wording before printing on a slide.

verification_levels.primary: read on the original page by us (none in this run)
verification_levels.secondary: number from search extraction of the source or from press/extension; original not opened
verification_levels.unverified: not confirmed; do not display as fact

facts.claim: Central Iowa Water Works supplies drinking water to about 600,000 people in central Iowa.
facts.source_title: High nitrate levels prompt a lawn watering ban for 600,000 people in central Iowa
facts.quote: High nitrate levels prompt a lawn watering ban for 600,000 people in central Iowa
facts.notes: Headline text. EPA CIWW case study (Oct 2026) also describes CIWW as serving approximately 600,000 people. CIWW was formed as a regional authority in 2024 (28E agreement) and began operating around 1 Jan 2025; it is a cooperative of 12 utilities, not a merger. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: The Fleur Drive nitrate removal facility can treat up to 10 million gallons a day, using 8 ion-exchange vessels (up to 7 run at once, 1 regenerates).
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: The facility includes eight treatment vessels and can process up to 10 million gallons of water per day.
facts.notes: Official CIWW FAQ page. Older DMWW explainer rates each vessel at 1.4 MGD (8 x 1.4 = 11.2), so 10 MGD is the operational figure. Runs when source-water nitrate threatens the 10 mg/L finished-water limit; it is blended with untreated water. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: In 2025 the nitrate removal facility ran (partly or fully) on 112 days; it was turned off on 8 Aug 2025.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works running nitrate removal facility, rare in January (KCCI report reprinted)
facts.quote: ran in part or fully for 112 days in spring and summer 2025
facts.notes: A mid-Aug 2025 CIWW release also said 112 days (an Aug 7 article said 111). IPR 2026-01-12 only says 'over 100 days'. Facility ran 68 days in 2024. Concept doc 'more than 110 days' is correct. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: CIWW's first-ever lawn-watering ban (Stage III) began 12 June 2025 because nitrate in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers was near record levels and nitrate removal was already at full capacity.
facts.source_title: CIWW Issues Lawn Watering Ban Effective Immediately
facts.quote: nitrate concentrations in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers have climbed to near record levels
facts.notes: Trigger: CIWW needed to limit river water used in treatment; NRF had run >55 days, all nitrate removal at full capacity; lawn watering ~40% of summer demand (Madsen). One release is dated June 13. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: The 2025 ban was first eased for residential customers on 22 July 2025.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa lawn watering ban lifted: Lawn watering schedule
facts.notes: Phased: residential first, commercial later.

facts.claim: CIWW ended the Stage III lawn-watering ban on 7 Aug 2025 (moved to Stage I, voluntary 25% cut); all restrictions ended 15 Aug 2025.
facts.source_title: CIWW ends Stage III lawn irrigation ban, implements Stage I voluntary 25 percent reduction in watering
facts.notes: KCCI: technical committee voted 15 Aug 2025 to resume normal irrigation; CIWW 'exits the water shortage program' release 18 Aug 2025. IWLA's 'June 12 to July 31, 49 days' is WRONG; IPR published a correction that the ban ended in August.

facts.claim: The mandatory 2025 Stage III lawn-watering ban lasted 56 days (12 Jun - 7 Aug 2025); for homes the full ban lasted 40 days (to 22 Jul).
facts.source_title: Derived from CIWW ban start/end releases
facts.notes: Our arithmetic from ban_2025_start and ban_2025_end. Residential full-ban days = 40. Any water restriction (Stage I-III) 30 May - 15 Aug = 77 days.

facts.claim: CIWW imposed its second mandatory lawn-watering ban on 8 June 2026, covering about 600,000 people.
facts.source_title: High nitrate levels prompt a lawn watering ban for 600,000 people in central Iowa
facts.notes: Preceded by a voluntary 50% outdoor-use cut requested late May 2026 (KCRG 2026-05-27). CIWW page: as of 8 Jun 2026 Raccoon >10 mg/L for 136 days, Des Moines River 117 days, infiltration gallery 86 days; NRF running ~95% of the year.

facts.claim: All customers moved off the 2026 lawn-watering ban (Stage III to Stage II) on 20 July 2026; all restrictions ended 27 July 2026.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works Transitions All Customers to Stage II Water Use Restrictions
facts.quote: Effective July 20, 2026, residential, commercial, and governmental customers may resume outdoor irrigation
facts.notes: A 1 Jul 2026 CIWW release began a phased easing (ban kept for commercial/governmental customers), so residential customers likely left the ban on 1 Jul. Technical committee ended all restrictions 27 Jul 2026. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: The 2026 mandatory lawn-watering ban lasted 42 days for all customers (8 Jun - 20 Jul 2026); about 23 days for homes if they were released 1 Jul.
facts.source_title: Derived from CIWW 2026 releases
facts.notes: Our arithmetic. Any restriction (8 Jun - 27 Jul) = 49 days. Residential release date (1 Jul vs 20 Jul) conflicts between sources.

facts.claim: To fully lift the 2025 ban, CIWW said at least one source must read 10 mg/L nitrate or less; it later kept the ban until both rivers showed a steady downward trend.
facts.source_title: Lawn watering ban remains despite Des Moines, Raccoon rivers recording nitrates under EPA drinking standard
facts.publisher: Des Moines Register via Yahoo News
facts.quote: at least one water source must record nitrate concentrations at 10 mg/L or less
facts.notes: 2026 lift criterion not found. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.source_title: CIWW Technical Committee minutes 2026-01-14 / later TC report

facts.claim: A Polk County-commissioned, 2-year study by 16 scientists (CISWRA, July 2025) attributed roughly 70-80% of nitrate in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers to agriculture (about 40% surplus fertilizer).
facts.source_title: Polk County research report confirms nitrate in rivers directly tied to agriculture
facts.publisher: Yahoo News / Iowa PBS Market to Market
facts.notes: Iowa PBS summary: >70% agricultural; 40% surplus fertilizer, 20% manure, 20% soybean-fixed. Axios 2026-08-18: manure 12-19%, cities 1.5-2%. Quote the report itself before using a single number.

facts.claim: In an average year, an Iowa acre of corn or soybeans loses about 30 lb of nitrogen as nitrate to waterways.
facts.source_title: The Science Behind Nitrate Transport
facts.notes: Range: ISU Gilmore City drainage site averaged ~36 lb N/ac at 150-160 lb N fertilizer, varying 0.9-94 lb/ac by weather; ~15-20 lb/ac even with no N. ISU Extension: normal 15-25, wet springs 40-50 lb/ac. Corn and soybean losses are similar.

facts.claim: In a 14-year USDA-ARS tile-drainage experiment near Ames, a cereal rye cover crop cut nitrate load by 57% (concentration by 59%).
facts.source_title: USDA ARS publication 333537 (Kaspar et al., broadcast rye/oat cover crops)
facts.quote: Over 14 years a cereal rye cover crop reduced nitrate concentrations by 59% and nitrate load by 57%.
facts.notes: USDA-ARS (Kaspar), not Iowa State; 14 years, not 15. Kaspar et al. 2007 JEQ (4 yr): 61% load, 59% conc. Kaspar et al. 2012 AWM: rye 48%, oat 26% (concentration). Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: At other Iowa sites, Kaspar reports rye cover crops cut nitrate 15-48% (on-farm 2016: 40% lower load). Effects depend on rye growth, soil, weather and drainage timing.
facts.source_title: Winter Cover Crop Impacts on Erosion and Nitrate Losses in Tile Drainage (Kaspar SARE presentation)
facts.notes: The concept doc's '22-48%' was NOT found; the source found gives 15-48%. Use 15-48%.

facts.claim: Iowa's Nutrient Reduction Strategy science assessment estimates a cereal rye cover crop cuts nitrate-N in drainage by 31% on average.
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment (Table, nitrogen practices)
facts.notes: Table entry '31 (29)' with corn yield '-6 (7)'. Measures concentration, not N-applied. Iowa Soybean Assn. (2026) cites a 27% INRS cover-crop average; Iowa Farm Bureau cites 28-31%. Not confirmed whether the Feb 2025 INRS update changed the value.

facts.claim: Standard deviation of the INRS rye cover crop nitrate reduction: 29 percentage points (very variable).
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment
facts.notes: Inferred: INRS tables report 'mean (SD)'. Minnesota's science assessment describes Iowa's fall-to-spring value as '6 ± 25%', supporting that the parentheses are SDs. A search tool misread '31 (29)' as 31% N / 29% P; ignore that reading.

facts.claim: INRS: oat cover crop cuts nitrate-N about 28% (SD 2).
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment
facts.notes: 28% supported only by secondary '28-31%' ranges (Iowa Farm Bureau, 2020 workshop slides); SD 2 from memory of the table, not confirmed.

facts.claim: INRS: an extended rotation (at least 2 years of alfalfa in a 4-5 yr rotation) cuts nitrate-N by 42% on average (SD 12).
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment
facts.notes: Table '42 (12)'; corn yield '7 (7)'. Iowa Capital Dispatch (2025-02-07) on the 2025 update: three-year extended rotation reduces nitrate-N in tile drainage by 42% on average.

facts.claim: INRS: retiring row-crop land to CRP cuts nitrate-N by 85% (SD 9); perennial energy crops by 72% (SD 23).
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment
facts.quote: 85% reduction in nitrate-N concentration with conversion to CRP from row-crop production
facts.notes: Perennial energy crops '72 (23)'. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: INRS: moving N application from fall to spring pre-plant cuts nitrate-N about 6% (SD 25); a nitrification inhibitor with fall anhydrous about 9% (SD 19).
facts.source_title: Iowa Science Assessment of Nonpoint Source Practices (NRS2)
facts.notes: Minnesota science assessment: Iowa 'originally recommended a 6 ± 25%' value and current Iowa value is lower. ISU NRS tracking v4 gives 5% for inhibitors (concentration). Sidedress vs spring pre-plant ~4%.

facts.claim: INRS: reducing N rate to the MRTN cuts nitrate-N about 10%.
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy: science assessment
facts.notes: Not confirmed in this session (value depends on starting rate). Science assessment text confirms rate reduction and cover crops have the greatest N-management potential.

facts.claim: INRS: woodchip bioreactors remove about 43% of nitrate load from treated drainage.

facts.claim: NRCS EQIP pays about $74/acre in Iowa (FY2026, regular rate) for a single-species cover crop (practice 340); about $89/acre for historically underserved producers.
facts.source_title: EQIP and CSP After the 2025 Budget Law: What Changed and How to Apply
facts.notes: Official FY26 Iowa Scenario Booklet (NRCS, 2026-04-28, https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2026-04/FY26%20FA%20Program%20Scenario%20Booklet_April%2028%202026.pdf) snippet shows 340 Single Species 89.20 and Multi-Species 93.05 — consistent with 89.20 being the HU rate (=74.34 x 90/75). Multi-species regular $77.54. Regular = 75% of cost. Confirm in the booklet before display.

facts.claim: NRCS EQIP pays about $11.53/acre in Iowa (FY2026, regular rate) for basic conservation crop rotation (practice 328); $13.84 for historically underserved.
facts.source_title: EQIP and CSP After the 2025 Budget Law: What Changed and How to Apply
facts.notes: Third-party only; ratio 13.84/11.53 = 1.20 matches the 90%/75% rule, but not seen in the NRCS booklet. Verify.

facts.claim: Custom drilling of cover crop seed in Iowa averaged $19.05/acre in 2026 (aerial seeding $14.70/acre).
facts.source_title: 2026 Iowa Farm Custom Rate Survey (Ag Decision Maker A3-10)
facts.notes: Drilling range $9-25; 2025 survey $18.30. Seeding service only, excludes seed.

facts.claim: Cereal rye seed costs roughly $15-30/acre; seed + seeding + termination typically $25-60/acre.
facts.source_title: Cover crop economics (ISU A1-88, July 2026; secondary summaries)
facts.notes: ISU A1-88 assumes 112 lb/ac (2 bu) seeding rate; seed price ~$0.25/lb (Aug 2026 snapshot, non-ISU) gives ~$28/ac at 112 lb, ~$15 at 60 lb. A1-88 snippet mentions '$41.65 per acre' — ambiguous (possibly total). ISU A1-92 lists rye seed ~$25/ac. Open A1-88 before using one number.

facts.claim: Iowa anhydrous ammonia averaged $1,096/ton in May 2026 (USDA AMS), which is about $0.67 per lb of N.
facts.source_title: Iowa Production Cost Report (Bi-Weekly), report 2863
facts.notes: Conversion ours: anhydrous is 82% N, 1 ton = 1,640 lb N; $1,095.83/1,640 = $0.668 (range $0.625-0.701). May 2025: $788/ton = $0.480/lb N. Urea May 2026 $870/ton (46% N) = $0.946/lb N. National AMS avg week ending 2 Oct 2026 $945/ton = $0.576/lb N; DTN late Sept $977. No Oct/Nov 2026 Iowa report found. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).

facts.claim: The EPA drinking-water limit (MCL) for nitrate is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen, set to protect infants under six months from blue baby syndrome (methemoglobinemia).
facts.source_title: What Are U.S. Standards and Regulations for Nitrates and Nitrites Exposure? (CSEM)
facts.notes: Equivalent to ~45 mg/L as nitrate ion. EPA reassessment of nitrate health risks announced 2023; outcome not confirmed. EPA: infants who drink water above the MCL 'could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die' (wording via UNL G1784).

facts.claim: Iowa Women's Health Study analyses (NCI) found higher thyroid, ovarian, bladder and kidney cancer risk with higher long-term public-water nitrate, but no link to colorectal or pancreatic cancer in that cohort.
facts.source_title: Water contaminants and cancer risk: arsenic, disinfection byproducts, and nitrate
facts.quote: women with higher average nitrate levels in public water supplies had increased risks of thyroid, ovarian, bladder, and kidney cancers
facts.notes: Associations, not proof of cause. Other studies (cited by Iowa Environmental Council 2024/2025, advocacy) link colorectal cancer to levels below 10 mg/L. Wording: 'studies have found associations'. Quote via web-search extraction of this page; page itself not opened (session network blocks direct fetch).
